name: Independent on Sunday cryptic crossword No 1,774

entries.clue: Think around 150 needed to show strength (6)

indicatorNotes.around: 'around' means surrounding, so the word for think wraps itself round the number

blocks.note: to muse is to think things over
Roman numerals: C is 100, L is 50

annotation.surface: Someone pondering a hundred and fifty of something before they can prove their strength.
annotation.walkthrough: Numbers in cryptic clues are very often Roman numerals rather than quantities, which is what turns this sensible-sounding sentence into letters.
annotation.definitionFit: Muscle is a common synonym for physical power, as in 'put some muscle into it'.

entries.clue: Be afraid of the sea monster, ultimately (4)

indicatorNotes.ultimately: 'ultimately' means in the end, so each word gives up only its final letter

blocks.note: the final letters of the four words

annotation.surface: A warning to be scared of a sea monster, when all is said and done.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Be afraid of' reads as one phrase, but 'of' is needed for the wordplay, so the definition stops at 'Be afraid'.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain verb synonym: to be afraid is to fear, and both take the thing dreaded as object.

entries.clue: Band of two meeting obstacle (8)

blocks.note: a brace is a pair, as of pheasants
an old word for hindrance, kept in 'without let or hindrance'

annotation.surface: Two members of a band run into some obstacle.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Band' looks like a musical group, but it is a ring of metal worn on the wrist.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by description: this piece of jewellery is a band that circles the wrist.

entries.clue: Wrongly take article, one acquired on memorable day (6)

indicatorNotes.acquired: the article acquires the one, taking it in so it ends up inside
indicatorNotes.on: in a down clue, one part placed on another sits above it, so the day goes last

blocks.note: the definite article
the Roman numeral for one
VE Day, 8 May 1945, Victory in Europe

annotation.surface: Someone wrongly takes an article they came by on a day to remember.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Memorable day' tempts you toward EVE, but the answer has room only for VE: Victory in Europe Day, marking the end of the Second World War in Europe.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: stealing is taking what is not yours, the wrong kind of taking.

entries.clue: Cheap yet tailored possible headgear for pirate? (8)

indicatorNotes.tailored: a tailored garment has been cut and reshaped, so these letters are refashioned too

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 8 letters

annotation.surface: A cheap but well-made hat for a pirate.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark admits that the answer is only loosely headgear: it is worn on the head, but it is no hat.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example with a wink: the patch over one eye is the pirate's trademark, worn on the head.

entries.clue: Issue's about 101 descendants (6)

indicatorNotes.about: 'about' means around, so the offspring word is placed around the number

blocks.note: issue means offspring, such as sons
Roman numerals: C is 100, I is 1

annotation.surface: A problem involving about a hundred and one descendants.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Issue' looks like a problem, but in the old legal sense it means children.
annotation.definitionFit: A near synonym: scions are the younger members of a line, especially of a noble family.

entries.clue: Coin has the middle part raised (4)

indicatorNotes.part: the answer is only a part of the words that follow, sitting inside them
indicatorNotes.raised: in a down clue, raising letters lifts the bottom to the top, so they read upwards

blocks.note: sitting inside thE MIDdle

annotation.surface: A coin whose central section is embossed.
annotation.walkthrough: 'The middle part' looks like an instruction to take a central letter, but it points at letters lying across those two words, which are then read upwards.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: this is the American ten-cent coin.

entries.clue: Chances to host dance for weirdos (8)

indicatorNotes.to host: a host takes guests in, so the dance ends up inside the chances

blocks.note: the odds are the chances of something happening
a ball is a formal dance

annotation.surface: Opportunities to throw a dance for the local eccentrics.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a charity event for eccentrics, and the answer really would be the guests.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain informal synonym: both words mean eccentric, peculiar people.

entries.clue: Phantom hunter lay prepared (9)

indicatorNotes.prepared: something prepared has been made up from raw ingredients, as these letters are

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 9 letters

annotation.surface: A ghost hunter lies in wait, all set.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Phantom' reads as a noun here, but it works as an adjective, as in a phantom limb.
annotation.definitionFit: An adjectival synonym: ghostly, not belonging to this world.

entries.clue: The Parisian abandons almost freezing infant? (5)

indicatorNotes.abandons: to abandon is to leave, so the French article leaves the word it was in

blocks.note: cooled nearly to freezing point
the French for 'the', taken out

annotation.surface: A Frenchman walks out on a baby who is nearly frozen.
annotation.walkthrough: 'The Parisian' means 'the' in French. The question mark admits the definition is by example: a child need not be an infant.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: an infant is one kind of young person, the youngest kind.

entries.clue: Craft Centre occupied by a criminal case (7)

indicatorNotes.occupied by: an occupied building has people living inside, so the centre word has letters inside it
indicatorNotes.case: a case is the outside of something, so only the first and last letters

blocks.note: the core is the centre
as written
the outer letters of CriminaL

annotation.surface: A craft centre broken into by a criminal case.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Craft Centre' reads as a place for arts and crafts, but 'Craft' is a boat and 'Centre' starts the wordplay. The answer is a small round wicker boat of Wales and Ireland.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a craft is any boat, and this is a small round one.

entries.clue: Saw dog restrained by lead (7)

indicatorNotes.restrained by: the dog is held in by the metal, as a dog is held by a lead, so it goes inside

blocks.note: a stock name for a dog
the chemical symbol for lead

annotation.surface: Someone spotted a dog held back on its leash.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Saw' looks like a verb and 'lead' like a leash, but a saw is an old saying and lead is the metal.
annotation.definitionFit: An old sense of 'saw': a traditional saying, as in 'the old saw'.

entries.clue: Enthusiastic traveller initially following meanders of Blue Nile (9)

indicatorNotes.initially: 'initially' means at first, so only the word's opening letter
indicatorNotes.following: one thing following another comes after it, so this letter goes last
indicatorNotes.meanders of: a meandering river winds about, so the river's letters wander into a new order

blocks.note: the river's letters rearranged
the opening letter of Traveller

annotation.surface: A keen traveller follows the winding course of the Blue Nile.
annotation.walkthrough: The T is written first in the clue but goes last, because it is following the rearranged river.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: bubbling over with enthusiasm, from the Latin for boiling up.

entries.clue: See 27
Hamlet's prop that could move boat on air (5)

indicatorNotes.on air: something on air is broadcast, so it is heard rather than read

blocks.note: to propel a boat with oars

annotation.surface: A stage prop in Hamlet that might propel a boat through the air.
annotation.walkthrough: In the graveyard scene Hamlet holds up the bones of the jester Yorick. 'On air' tempts the reader to picture flying.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by allusion: Yorick's bone is the most famous prop in Hamlet.

entries.clue: Perhaps 22's 27 14 isn't one such? (1,1,1)

blocks.note: the cross-references spell out Who's police box: the TARDIS of Doctor Who
the TARDIS flies, but everyone knows exactly what it is, so it is not unidentified

annotation.surface: A puzzle over whether a famous time machine counts as something mysterious in the sky.
annotation.walkthrough: Doctor Who is a long-running BBC science-fiction series whose time machine is disguised as a blue police box. It is a flying object, just not an unidentified one.
annotation.definitionFit: The initials stand for unidentified flying object, and the clue plays on the TARDIS being identified.

entries.clue: Left with bill for setter, obtained on demand (7)

indicatorNotes.for: 'for' means in place of, so the bill takes the setter's spot

blocks.note: went out
a bill passed by Parliament becomes an Act
setters refer to themselves as I or me; this I is swapped out

annotation.surface: Someone walked out with the bill for the crossword setter, paid on the spot.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bill for setter' looks like an invoice, but it is an instruction to swap one piece for another.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to exact payment is to demand it and get it.

entries.clue: He needs Mike actively involved (8)

indicatorNotes.actively: letters that act lively move about rather than stay in order

blocks.note: anagram fodder
M in the NATO phonetic alphabet

annotation.surface: A man needs his friend Mike to take part.
annotation.walkthrough: Mike reads as a person's name, but it is the radio code word for a letter.
annotation.definitionFit: A near synonym: caught in a mesh or net, so entangled or involved.

entries.clue: American national swimmer (3)

blocks.note: a standard abbreviation for American
the nation, the United Kingdom

annotation.surface: An American competing in the national swimming team.
annotation.walkthrough: The swimmer is a bird: these northern seabirds dive and swim underwater to catch fish.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: this seabird swims and dives expertly.

entries.clue: Loses possession of illegally gained ball, landing at back of net (4,4)

annotation.definition: ball, landing at back of net

blocks.note: letting go of something
slang for stolen

annotation.surface: A player loses control of a dodgy ball, which lands at the back of the net.
annotation.walkthrough: The football surface misleads: this is tennis, and 'back of net' is the far side of it, where a delicate stroke falls just over.
annotation.definitionFit: A tennis term: a soft stroke that barely clears the net and lands just beyond it.

entries.clue: Disturbs hospital signs (7)

blocks.note: the map and road-sign symbol for hospital
direction signs

annotation.surface: Hospital signage that upsets people.
annotation.walkthrough: The answer is the verb, not the farm tool or the school: to distress someone deeply.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a harrowing experience deeply disturbs.

entries.clue: Put another way, he shared crackers (8)

indicatorNotes.crackers: crackers means crazy, and crazy letters do not stay in order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 8 letters

annotation.surface: In other words, he split the Christmas crackers with someone.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Crackers' sits at the end like a noun he shared, but it is the adjective for crazy.
annotation.definitionFit: A near synonym: old material reworded or recycled has been put another way.

entries.clue: How disorganised is international body! (1,1,1)

indicatorNotes.disorganised: disorganised things are out of order, as these letters are

blocks.note: anagram fodder

annotation.surface: An exclamation at how chaotic an international organisation is.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is a jibe at bureaucracy, and the joke is that the body is itself hiding in 'How'.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the World Health Organization is a United Nations agency.

entries.clue: See 31
Like a pickle? (6)

blocks.note: the verb, to enjoy something
a chunky, tangy sauce served with food

annotation.surface: Asking whether something resembles a pickle.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Like' reads as 'similar to', but it is the verb meaning enjoy.
annotation.definitionFit: The word means both to enjoy greatly and a pickled condiment such as sweetcorn relish.

entries.clue: Does your hairdresser take some of this from your gross income in the States? (3,3,3)

annotation.definition: Does your hairdresser take some of this from your gross income in the States?

blocks.note: the surface reading: a trim from the crown of your head

blocks.clueFragment: from your gross income in the States?
blocks.note: the American idiom for money deducted before anything else

annotation.surface: Wondering whether the barber takes a cut of your pay before tax, American style.
annotation.walkthrough: The phrase works twice: a barber's light trim, and the American business sense of deductions taken first from gross pay.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom with two readings: a haircut taken from the crown, and money deducted from gross income.

entries.clue: Ousting everyone, beat Dean maybe (6)

indicatorNotes.Ousting: to oust is to throw out, so the everyone word is removed

blocks.note: to get in first, beat someone to it
all of them, removed from the end

annotation.surface: A college dean, perhaps, beaten after everyone was thrown out.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Dean' looks like a person, but it is a place: the ancient royal woodland of Dean in Gloucestershire, western England.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example, flagged by 'maybe': Dean is one of England's great woodlands.

entries.clue: Band has hit with antiquated communication equipment (6,3)

blocks.note: the rock band fronted by Sting
to box is to hit

annotation.surface: A band has a hit record made on antiquated equipment.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Band' and 'hit' paint a pop chart. The answer is a British street kiosk holding a telephone for calling officers, long obsolete and famous as the disguise of Doctor Who's TARDIS.
annotation.definitionFit: A description: the kiosk was a public telephone link to officers, now outdated.

entries.clue: Provides for issue primarily (7)

blocks.note: reads like dealing with a problem, but issue means offspring
reads like 'mainly', but it means first, in the earliest days of life

annotation.surface: A policy statement: it deals mainly with one particular matter.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Primarily' tempts the solver to look for first letters, but there are none to take; it simply means at the very start of life.
annotation.definitionFit: A description: a mother feeding her newborn young with milk provides for her issue first of all.

entries.clue: Beware of cut (not with right)! (4)

indicatorNotes.not with: the cut word is taken not with, meaning without, the right letter

blocks.note: to slice
the abbreviation for right, removed

annotation.surface: A warning to watch out for a cut, provided it is not on the right.
annotation.walkthrough: The answer is Latin, said 'kay-vee', and was old British schoolboy slang shouted by a lookout when a teacher approached.
annotation.definitionFit: A Latin imperative borrowed into English school slang, meaning look out.

entries.clue: Relaxing start of recital with arrangement for flutes (7)

indicatorNotes.start of: the start of a word is its first letter, so the recital gives only that
indicatorNotes.arrangement for: a musical arrangement rewrites a piece for new instruments, and here it rewrites the letters

blocks.note: the opening letter of Recital
the instrument's letters rearranged

annotation.surface: A soothing recital that opens with a piece arranged for flutes.
annotation.walkthrough: The music surface is consistent throughout, and 'arrangement' works in both senses: a score for flutes and a reordering of letters.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain adjectival synonym: calm and soothing, full of rest.

entries.clue: Prometheus, for one, to dispense with God? (4-5)

blocks.note: to sack someone is to dispense with them
God as the creator of all things

annotation.surface: The myth of Prometheus defying the gods, recast as an attempt to do without God.
annotation.walkthrough: In Greek myth Prometheus stole flame from the gods for mankind. 'Dispense with' reads as doing without, but here it means sacking.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Prometheus gave humanity the gift of flame, so he is one such figure.

entries.clue: Unfinished silver collection for 1950s/60s icon (5)

indicatorNotes.Unfinished: something unfinished lacks its end, so the final letter goes
indicatorNotes.collection: a collection gathers things up in any order, so the letters are regrouped

blocks.note: the metal without its final letter

annotation.surface: An incomplete silver set made for a star of the fifties and sixties, like a disc award.
annotation.walkthrough: The King of rock and roll had his heyday in the 1950s and 60s, and the surface's silver suggests his record awards.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Presley is the defining pop icon of those two decades.

entries.clue: Nothing to be left unchanged in multinational group, concerning deliveries (9)

indicatorNotes.in: 'in' places the proofreader's word inside the group of nations

blocks.note: the letter that looks like zero
Brazil, Russia, India, China, grouped as emerging economies
the proofreader's mark meaning 'let it stand'

annotation.surface: No change allowed within an international group regarding shipments.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Deliveries' suggests parcels, but here it means births.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by allusion: the medical specialty of delivering babies.
